etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Latin hemisphaerium, from Ancient Greek ἡμισφαίριον (hēmisphaírion), from ἡμι- (hēmi-, “half”) + σφαῖρα (sphaîra, “sphere”). Equivalent to hemi- +‎ sphere. Displaced native Old English healftrendel (literally “half-sphere”).

definitions.definition: (astronomy, astrology) Half of the celestial sphere, as divided by either the ecliptic or the celestial equator [from 14th c.].
(figuratively) A realm or domain of activity [1503].

quote.citation: 1831, L[etitia] E[lizabeth] L[andon], Romance and Reality. […], volume III, London: Henry Colburn and Richard Bentley, […], →OCLC, pages 91–92:
quote.text: Love is the Columbus of our moral world, and opens, at some period or other, a new hemisphere to our view.

definitions.definition: (geography) Half of the Earth, such as the Northern Hemisphere, Southern Hemisphere, Western Hemisphere or Eastern Hemisphere, Land Hemisphere, Water Hemisphere etc. [1550s].
(geometry) Any half-sphere, formed by a plane intersecting the center of a sphere. [1580s].
(cartography) A map or projection of a celestial or terrestrial hemisphere [1706].
(anatomy) Either of the two halves of the cerebrum. [1804].
